questions.question_text: Demand in economics means the quantity of a good a consumer is:
options: Able and willing to buy at a given price in a given period
questions.explanation: Demand needs desire, ability to pay (purchasing power) and willingness, at a price and over a period.

questions.question_text: The difference between desire and demand is that demand is:
options: Desire backed by purchasing power and willingness to pay
questions.explanation: A desire without the ability to pay is not effective demand.

questions.question_text: The demand function is written as:
options: Dx = f(Px, Pr, Y, T, E)
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded depends on own price, related prices, income, tastes and expectations.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT a determinant of demand?
options: Cost of production of the seller
questions.explanation: Cost of production is a supply-side factor.

questions.question_text: If the price of tea (a substitute) rises, demand for coffee:
questions.explanation: Consumers shift to the cheaper substitute.

questions.question_text: If the price of cars (complement of petrol) rises sharply, demand for petrol:
questions.explanation: Complements are used together; demand moves in the opposite direction to the other's price.

questions.question_text: Normal goods are those whose demand:
questions.explanation: Examples: clothes, fruits, smartphones.

questions.question_text: Inferior goods are those whose demand:
questions.explanation: Examples: coarse cereals, low-quality bus travel.

questions.question_text: As income rises, demand for luxuries:
questions.explanation: Necessities rise by a smaller proportion.

questions.question_text: A favourable change in fashion for a product will:
questions.explanation: Tastes and fashions shift the demand curve.

questions.question_text: If consumers expect prices to rise in future, current demand will:
questions.explanation: People buy now to avoid higher future prices.

questions.question_text: An increase in population generally:
questions.explanation: More consumers mean larger total demand.

questions.question_text: If income is redistributed from rich to poor, demand for necessities generally:
questions.explanation: The poor spend a larger share of extra income on necessities.

questions.question_text: Derived demand is demand for a good because of:
options: Its use in producing another good (e.g., demand for steel)
questions.explanation: Direct demand is for final consumption, e.g., demand for rice.

questions.question_text: Composite demand exists when a good has:
options: More than one use (e.g., steel, milk)
questions.explanation: Demand is the sum of demand for each use.

questions.question_text: Joint demand is the demand for goods:
questions.explanation: They complement each other.

questions.question_text: Market demand is:
options: The sum of individual demands at each price
questions.explanation: It is the horizontal sum of individual demand curves.

questions.question_text: A demand schedule is:
options: A table showing quantities demanded at various prices
questions.explanation: It is the tabular form of demand.

questions.question_text: If three consumers demand 2, 3 and 5 units at a price, market demand at that price is:
A demand curve is:
options: A graph of price against quantity demanded
A graph of income against savings
A graph of cost against output
questions.explanation: It plots the demand schedule.

questions.question_text: The demand curve slopes downward mainly because of:
options: Diminishing marginal utility, income and substitution effects
questions.explanation: Lower prices raise quantity demanded.

questions.question_text: To derive an individual demand curve, one:
options: Plots price on the Y-axis and quantity on the X-axis from the schedule
questions.explanation: Join the plotted points.

questions.question_text: The market demand curve is obtained by:
options: Horizontal summation of individual demand curves
questions.explanation: Add quantities at each price.

questions.question_text: The market demand curve is flatter than individual curves because:
options: Quantities are added at each price, making the curve more responsive
questions.explanation: Summing quantities spreads the curve horizontally.

questions.question_text: The demand curve is derived from the MU curve because:
options: MU equals the price the consumer is willing to pay
questions.explanation: Willingness to pay for each unit measures MU, so the MU curve shows demand.

questions.question_text: The Law of Demand states that, other things constant, as price falls:
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.

questions.question_text: The law of demand is associated with:
questions.explanation: Marshall formally stated the law of demand.

questions.question_text: An assumption of the law of demand is:
questions.explanation: Other things (ceteris paribus) remain unchanged.

questions.question_text: A schedule where price rises Rs. 10, 8, 6 and quantity is 10, 20, 30 shows:
options: An inverse relation between price and quantity (law of demand)
questions.explanation: Lower price, higher quantity.

questions.question_text: The income effect in the law of demand is that a fall in price:
options: Raises real income, enabling more purchases
questions.explanation: A lower price raises purchasing power.

questions.question_text: The substitution effect means that when a good's price falls, consumers:
options: Substitute it for relatively costlier goods
questions.explanation: The cheaper good replaces others.

questions.question_text: DMU explains the law of demand because:
options: Consumers pay less for additional units as MU falls
questions.explanation: They buy more only when the price falls to match falling MU.

questions.question_text: A fall in price attracts new consumers because:
options: The good becomes affordable to those previously unable to buy
questions.explanation: Lower prices widen the market.

questions.question_text: Which is an exception to the law of demand?
questions.explanation: Others: Veblen goods, expectations of price rise, speculation.

questions.question_text: Giffen goods are an exception because:
options: Demand rises when price rises, as strong negative income effect dominates
questions.explanation: They are inferior goods; e.g., staple food for the very poor.

questions.question_text: Veblen goods are:
options: Prestige goods bought more when their price is higher
questions.explanation: Their high price gives status.

questions.question_text: Conspicuous consumption was propounded by:
questions.explanation: It describes buying for show.

questions.question_text: If consumers expect prices to rise further, they:
options: Buy more now even at higher prices, violating the law of demand
questions.explanation: Expectation of a price rise increases current demand.

questions.question_text: Speculative markets violate the law of demand because:
options: Buyers purchase more when prices are rising, expecting further gains
questions.explanation: Speculators chase rising prices.

questions.question_text: Demand for necessities:
options: Is not an exception; demand responds only slightly to price
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded still moves inversely with price, though only a little.

questions.question_text: Giffen goods differ from Veblen goods because Giffen goods are:
options: Inferior goods of the poor, while Veblen goods are prestige goods of the rich
questions.explanation: The reasons for the upward-sloping demand differ.

questions.question_text: Extension of demand means:
options: Fall in quantity due to a rise in price
Rise in quantity demanded due to fall in price
questions.explanation: It is a downward movement along the same demand curve.

questions.question_text: Contraction of demand means:
options: Fall in quantity demanded due to a rise in price
Rise in quantity due to a price fall
questions.explanation: It is an upward movement along the curve.

questions.question_text: An increase in demand means:
options: Rightward shift of the demand curve
questions.explanation: More is demanded at each price.

questions.question_text: A decrease in demand means:
options: Leftward shift of the demand curve
questions.explanation: Less is demanded at each price because of non-price factors.

questions.question_text: A change in quantity demanded is caused by a change in:
questions.explanation: A change in demand is caused by other factors.

questions.question_text: A change in quantity demanded is shown by:
options: Movement along the same demand curve
questions.explanation: Extension or contraction.

questions.question_text: A change in demand is shown by:
options: A shift of the demand curve
questions.explanation: Increase = right shift; decrease = left shift.

questions.question_text: Which causes an increase in demand?
options: Rise in income of consumers (normal good)
Fall in price of a substitute
Rise in price of a complement
questions.explanation: A rise in income of buyers of normal goods raises demand.

questions.question_text: Which causes a decrease in demand?
options: Rise in price of a complement
questions.explanation: A higher price of a complement lowers demand for the good.

questions.question_text: If the price of tea rises, demand for coffee:
questions.explanation: Tea and coffee are substitutes.

questions.question_text: If the price of petrol rises sharply, demand for cars:
questions.explanation: Petrol and cars are complements.

questions.question_text: If income rises, demand for an inferior good:
questions.explanation: People switch to superior goods.

questions.question_text: A fall in the price of apples raising apple purchases is:
questions.explanation: It is an extension of demand.

questions.question_text: A rise in income raising demand for smartphones is:
questions.explanation: Non-price factor changes demand.

questions.question_text: Elasticity of demand measures:
options: Responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in a determinant
questions.explanation: It is the degree of responsiveness.

questions.question_text: The concept of elasticity was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Marshall introduced it in Principles of Economics.

questions.question_text: The types of elasticity of demand are:
questions.explanation: Based on price, income and price of related goods.

questions.question_text: Price elasticity of demand is:
options: Change in price ÷ change in quantity
% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price
questions.explanation: Ed = %ΔQ / %ΔP (in absolute value).

questions.question_text: The five degrees of price elasticity are:
options: Perfectly elastic, highly elastic, unitary, less elastic, perfectly inelastic

questions.question_text: Perfectly elastic demand has Ed equal to:
questions.explanation: The demand curve is horizontal.

questions.question_text: Perfectly inelastic demand has Ed equal to:
questions.explanation: The demand curve is vertical.

questions.question_text: Unitary elastic demand means Ed equals:
questions.explanation: Percentage change in quantity equals percentage change in price.

questions.question_text: Relatively elastic demand means Ed is:
questions.explanation: Quantity changes proportionately more than price.

questions.question_text: Relatively inelastic demand means Ed is:
questions.explanation: Quantity changes proportionately less than price.

questions.question_text: In the percentage method, Ed equals:
questions.explanation: Compare the percentage changes in quantity and price.

questions.question_text: In the total outlay method, if price falls and total expenditure rises, demand is:
questions.explanation: Expenditure moves opposite to price when demand is elastic.

questions.question_text: Elasticity at a point on a straight-line demand curve equals:
questions.explanation: Ed = lower segment / upper segment at that point.

questions.question_text: On a straight-line demand curve, Ed = 1 at the:
questions.explanation: Upper and lower segments are equal.

questions.question_text: On a linear demand curve, Ed is _____ at the Y-intercept and _____ at the X-intercept:
questions.explanation: Ed falls as one moves down the curve.

questions.question_text: The arc elasticity formula uses:
Price falls from Rs. 10 to Rs. 8; quantity rises from 100 to 120. Ed (percentage method) is:
Price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 25; quantity falls from 80 to 60. Ed is:
Price falls from Rs. 5 to Rs. 4; quantity rises from 50 to 80. Ed is:
Price Rs. 50, quantity 100; price rises to Rs. 55 and quantity falls to 95. Ed is:
A 10% rise in price causes a 25% fall in demand. Ed is:
If Ed = 2 and price falls by 5%, quantity demanded rises by:
If total expenditure rises when price falls, Ed is:
questions.explanation: Demand is elastic.

questions.question_text: If total expenditure is unchanged when price rises, Ed is:
questions.explanation: Demand is unitary elastic.

questions.question_text: Using the arc method with P1 = 10, Q1 = 40, P2 = 8, Q2 = 50, Ed is:
Which factor affects price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Others: nature of good, income share, time period.

questions.question_text: Demand for salt is inelastic because it is:
options: A necessity with no close substitute and a small share of income
questions.explanation: Price changes hardly alter consumption.

questions.question_text: Demand for luxury cars is elastic because:
options: They are costly with many substitutes and can be postponed
questions.explanation: Buyers respond strongly to price changes.

questions.question_text: Over a longer time period, demand generally becomes:
questions.explanation: Consumers have time to find substitutes.

questions.question_text: The more substitutes a good has, the _____ its demand:
questions.explanation: Consumers can easily switch.

questions.question_text: Goods taking a large share of income have _____ demand:
questions.explanation: Price changes noticeably affect budgets.

questions.question_text: Income elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: Ey = %ΔQ / %ΔY.

questions.question_text: A good is a luxury if Ey is:
questions.explanation: Necessities have Ey between 0 and 1.

questions.question_text: Income rises 10% and quantity rises 15%. Ey is:
Cross elasticity of demand measures:
options: Responsiveness of demand for X to a change in the price of Y
questions.explanation: Ec = %ΔQx / %ΔPy.

questions.question_text: Cross elasticity is positive for _____ and negative for _____:
questions.explanation: A rise in the price of a substitute increases demand.

questions.question_text: Price of tea rises 20%, demand for coffee rises 10%. Ec is:
questions.explanation: 10/20 = 0.5, positive, so they are substitutes.

questions.question_text: When demand is elastic (Ed > 1), a price cut:
options: Raises TR and MR is positive
questions.explanation: Elastic demand means MR > 0 and TR rises as price falls.

questions.question_text: MR = P(1 − 1/Ed). If Ed = 2 and P = 10, MR is:
A monopolist never operates on the inelastic part of demand because there:
questions.explanation: With Ed < 1, MR < 0, which cannot equal positive MC.

questions.question_text: Elasticity helps the government in taxation because:
options: It shows which goods yield more revenue when taxed (inelastic goods)
questions.explanation: Taxing inelastic goods raises revenue with little fall in sales.

questions.question_text: A producer facing elastic demand should:
questions.explanation: TR rises when price falls under elastic demand.

questions.question_text: The paradox of poverty states that:
options: Larger crops may fetch lower total revenue for farmers because demand for farm produce is inelastic
questions.explanation: Price falls proportionately more than the quantity sold rises.

questions.question_text: The Marshall–Lerner condition states that devaluation improves the trade balance if:
options: Sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1
questions.explanation: Ed(x) + Ed(m) > 1.

questions.question_text: The incidence of a tax falls more on the side of the market that is:
questions.explanation: The less elastic side cannot easily avoid the tax and bears more of it.
